title: How To Make Time-Out A Stronger Consequence https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/08/28/how-to-make-time-out-a-stronger-consequence/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that a typical five-to-ten-minute time-out often isn't a strong enough consequence, and offers an eleven-step system for making it more effective. Key elements include teaching the time-out procedure thoroughly at the start of the year, enforcing it publicly and matter-of-factly, briefly telling students why they were sent, and then withholding lectures, scolding, or visible displeasure so responsibility stays with the student. He recommends letting students decide when they are ready to return by explaining their thinking, allowing considerably longer stretches than the conventional short window, and having them do the talking when they ask to rejoin the class. Once time-out ends, Linsin insists teachers should not hold a grudge and should welcome the student back as a full member of the class. He stresses that time-out is most powerful when it functions as both a physical and an emotional separation from a classroom students genuinely enjoy.
points: Teach and model the full time-out procedure during the first days of school so students know exactly what is expected.
Enforce time-out publicly and dispassionately, briefly stating the broken rule without lecturing, scolding, or showing displeasure.
Let students decide when they are ready to rejoin the class by explaining their thinking, rather than fixing the length in advance.
Allow time-out to run considerably longer than the standard five or ten minutes—twenty to thirty minutes or more if needed for genuine reflection.
Treat time-out as both a physical and emotional separation, which only works if students already enjoy being part of the classroom.
quotes: In other words, time-out needs to be about as much fun as dropping a dumbbell on your toes.
Your students must know exactly how to go to time-out, what they’re required to do once they’re there, and what they must do to rejoin their classmates.
Don’t add to it by lecturing, scolding, or showing displeasure. These methods weaken time-out by lifting the weight of accountability off of your students’ shoulders.
Most teachers remove students from time-out too soon. For most students, five or ten minutes won’t have the desired effect.
When a student says they’re ready to leave time-out, let them do the talking. If you’re satisfied with their level of contrition, smile and invite them back.
After completing time-out, allow the student to return to being a regular member of your classroom—in good standing. Don’t hold a grudge.
For time-out to be a strong consequence, it must be an emotional, as well as physical, separation.
